Lodz New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Łódź, Poland

Not demolished. Established in 1892 on land purchased by the industrialist Izrael Poznański — one of Łódź's leading entrepreneurs, later buried here himself alongside Rabbi Eljasz Chaim Majzel — this cemetery grew into one of the largest Jewish cemeteries in Europe, with roughly 160,000 tombstones across 42 hectares. Partially damaged during WWI by both local residents and Russian soldiers, it was later absorbed in part into the boundaries of the Łódź Ghetto in 1940; nearly 45,000 Jews who died in the ghetto were buried here before January 1945, in what became known as the 'ghetto field.' The cemetery has remained in continuous use by the Łódź Jewish community ever since — one of only about 20 still-active Jewish cemeteries in all of Poland — and was formally recognized as a Historical Monument by Polish presidential regulation in 2015. Łódź's Jewish community, which numbered over 156,000 (nearly 35 percent of the city) by 1921, was overwhelmingly murdered at the Chełmno and Auschwitz-Birkenau camps between 1942 and 1944; a Jewish community still exists in Łódź today.
